PCF: the Access Point takes control

With DCF a station never knows when it will transmit. To remove that randomness PCF was invented, the contention-free period.

In PCF the Access Point takes control of the medium and decides who transmits and when. The terminal does not wait for its turn by listening: the AP polls it, that is, asks whether it has anything to transmit.

The AP alternates between point control (PCF) and distributed control (DCF). A PCF followed by a DCF make up the repetition interval.
In DCF each station fights for the medium; in PCF the AP hands out the turns.
Beacon (B): management frame that the AP emits once every 100 ms. It is used to announce itself (that is how the OS builds the list of networks) and to announce the start of a PCF.
SIFS, PIFS and DIFS: who gets there first

Some stations may support PCF and others not. Those that don't carry on as in DCF: they listen and, when a free DIFS window opens, they try to transmit.

To keep that from happening in the middle of a PCF, shorter interframe intervals were chosen:

  • SIFS: the one that, in general, follows each operation.
  • PIFS: the one the AP waits if the polled station has nothing.

This way there is never a silence of DIFS duration, and no other station finds room to enter.
SIFS < PIFS < DIFS: whoever has to wait less keeps the medium.

During the PCF someone is always transmitting after a SIFS or, at most, a PIFS. The medium is never idle for a full DIFS: stations that do not support PCF keep listening, but cannot get in until the period ends.

The beacon announces the start of the PCF. After a SIFS, the AP sends a data frame (D1) and, along with it, a poll.

If the polled station has something to transmit, it sends its data frame plus the ACK for what it received (U1 + ACK).

After another SIFS, the AP does several operations in a single transmission: it sends data (D2), acknowledges what it received from the station (ACK) and polls the next one (poll).
Data, acknowledgment and polling travel together: that way no gap is left between frames.
No response, PIFS and end of period

The AP repeats the pattern: each time it sends something, it sends data, some acknowledgment (if needed) and the poll to the next station.

If the polled station has nothing to transmit, the AP waits a PIFS, transmits a new data frame and polls another one.

At the end, the AP announces the end of the contention-free period. The medium is left free for the terminals to compete again in DCF, where those that do not support PCF can also operate.
The AP receives the sender's frame and it is the AP that sends it to the destination.

Terminal and Access Point exchange frames in this format: MAC header, body (0 to 2312 bytes) and CRC. The network card driver presents it to the device as an Ethernet II frame.

The first field, Frame Control, expands into several subfields. Type and Subtype say what kind of frame it is:

  • Management: association, authentication, beacon.
  • Control: RTS, CTS, ACK.
  • Data.
The frames we have already seen (beacon, RTS, CTS, ACK) are told apart by the type that Frame Control marks.

The rest of Frame Control are one-bit flags:

  • More frag: the frame is fragmented. If the channel error probability is high, it is better to send small messages.
  • Retry: the frame is a retransmission.
  • Power mgmt: which power mode the station is in after transmitting.
  • More data: the AP tells the station it has more for it.
  • WEP: the data field is encrypted.
  • Order: order.
Retry in action: the ACK of a frame is lost → the sender thinks it did not arrive and resends it with Retry = 1 → the receiver, which already had it, recognizes it as a duplicate and discards it.

Two bits say whether the frame goes toward the distribution system or comes from it:

  • ToDS = 1: it is sent to the Access Point destined for a station in the distribution system.
  • FromDS = 1: the frame comes from the distribution system.

Depending on those two bits, what each Address field carries changes (table).

The rest: Duration (how much time the transmitting station needs), Sequence Control (indicates the fragment) and a 32-bit CRC.
Since the AP is always in the middle, two addresses are not enough: that is why there are up to four.
Address fields by ToDS and FromDS

DA: destination · SA: source · BSSID: identifies the AP's cell · RA / TA: who receives and who transmits over the air.
Duration is the time from which the others build their NAV.

To join a cell, a station completes three steps:

  • Synchronization: through the Access Point's beacon frames.
  • Authentication: exchange of information (key) between the AP and the terminal.
  • Association: the terminal is linked to the AP. From here on it can transmit.

To protect the network, WEP (Wired Equivalent Privacy) was defined: it prevents interception of the information and limits which terminals access the AP. Today it is almost never used: it could be bypassed by brute force.
Synchronize, authenticate, associate: only after the third step can data be sent.

Chronologically:

  • 802.11b: the first solution adopted massively. 2.4 GHz, up to 11 Mbps, DSSS modulation.
  • 802.11a: 54 Mbps with OFDM, but in 5 GHz, which did not turn out better (it required larger antennas).
  • 802.11g: the 54 Mbps in the 2.4 GHz band, with OFDM or DSSS.
  • 802.11n: uses both bands, up to 600 Mbps with OFDM.
Each standard sought more speed: first by changing the modulation, then by adding bands and antennas.
802.11n allows antenna diversity: with multiple antennas, multiple streams can be transmitted simultaneously.
PCF and frames at a glance

• PCF: the AP polls the stations; it alternates with DCF in each repetition interval.
  • Beacon every 100 ms: announces the network and the start of the PCF.
  • SIFS < PIFS < DIFS: during the PCF no one else gets in.
  • 802.11 frame: Frame Control (type, ToDS / FromDS, flags), duration, up to 4 addresses, CRC.
  • Joining a cell: synchronization, authentication, association.

Why can't a station that does not support PCF transmit during the contention-free period?
Because it never finds the medium idle for a DIFS: frames follow each other every SIFS or PIFS
SIFS and PIFS are shorter than DIFS, so during the PCF there is never a silence long enough for it to get in.
A frame's ACK is lost and the sender sends it again. Which Frame Control flag lets the receiver discard the duplicate?
Retry indicates the frame is a retransmission; it exists precisely to discard duplicates when the ACK was lost.
In what order does a station join a cell?
First it synchronizes with the beacons, then it exchanges the key (authentication) and finally it links to the AP (association).
Contention-free period: the AP controls the medium and polls the stations. It alternates with DCF: PCF + DCF = repetition interval.
